terms.definition: A tendency to search for information that supports our preconceptions and to ignore or distort contradictory evidence.
The tendency to believe, after an event has occurred, that you could have predicted the outcome in advance (“I knew it all along” phenomenon)
The tendency to be more confident than correct—to overestimate the accuracy of our beliefs and judgments.
The scientific study of behavior and mental processes.
A descriptive technique in which one individual or group is studied in depth in the hope of revealing universal principles.
A sample of participants selected because they are easy to access or readily available rather than randomly chosen from the population, which can make it less representative of the general population
The influence of the experimenter's expectations or preferences on the outcome of a research study.
The extent to which research findings can be applied to larger populations, other settings, or different groups beyond the participants in the study
A specific, testable prediction about the relationship between two or more variables
A statistical technique that combines and analyzes the results of multiple independent studies on the same topic to determine an overall trend, conclusion, or effect size
Observing and recording behavior in naturally occurring situations without trying to manipulate and control the situation.
A highly specific, precise description of the exact procedures (operations) and measurements used to define a variable in a research study
A process in which other experts in the same field evaluate a researcher’s study before it is published to ensure the research is accurate, credible, and scientifically sound
All those in a group being studied, from which samples may be drawn.
A sample that fairly represents a population because each member has an equal chance of inclusion.
The process of repeating a research study to see if the same results can be obtained again, confirming that findings are reliable, accurate, and not due to chance
A sample that accurately reflects the characteristics of the population as a whole.
A subset of individuals chosen from a larger set (a population).
A flawed sampling process that produces an unrepresentative sample.
An error that occurs when research participants provide inaccurate, distorted, or dishonest answers on surveys, questionnaires, or self-report inventorie
The tendency for survey participants to answer questions in a manner that will be viewed favorably by others rather than truthfully.
A technique for ascertaining the self-reported attitudes or behaviors of a particular group, usually by questioning a representative, random sample of the group.
An explanation using an integrated set of principles that organizes observations and predicts behaviors or events.
A factor other than the independent variable that might produce an effect in an experiment.
In an experiment, the group not exposed to the treatment; contrasts with the experimental group and serves as a comparison.
A measure of the extent to which two variables change together, and thus of how well either variable predicts the other.
A statistical measure that quantifies both the strength and the direction between two variables (from -1.0 to +1.0)
The outcome factor; the variable that may change in response to manipulations of the independent variable.
A situation in correlational research where it is known that two variables are related, but it is unclear which variable is causing the other.
An experimental procedure in which both the research participants and the research staff are ignorant (blind) about whether the research participants have received the treatment or a placebo.
A research method in which an investigator manipulates one or more factors to observe the effect on some behavior or mental process
In an experiment, the group exposed to the treatment, that is, to one version of the independent variable.
The requirement that for any hypothesis, theory, or claim to be considered scientifically valid, it must be testable in a way that allows for the possibility of being proven false
The perception of a relationship between two variables when no real relationship exists or when the relationship is weaker than it seems
The experimental factor that is manipulated; the variable whose effect is being studied.
A statistical relationship between two variables where they move in opposite (inverse) directions.
Research methods that do not involve manipulation of independent variables
An inactive substance, dummy treatment, or fake procedure that has no inherent physiological or therapeutic value

A psychological and physiological phenomenon where a participant experiences real changes in behavior, mood, or health purely due to their expectations of a treatment, rather than the treatment itself
A statistical relationship between two variables where they move in the same direction
Assigning participants to experimental and control groups by chance, thus minimizing preexisting differences between the different groups.
The tendency for extreme or unusual scores to fall back (regress) toward their average.
A graphed cluster of dots, each of which represents the values of two variables. The slope suggests the direction of the relationship.
An experimental procedure in which the research participants are ignorant (blind) about whether they have received the treatment or a placebo.
A situation in correlational research where an unmeasured, outside variable is responsible for the observed relationship between two other variables
Anything that can vary and is feasible and ethical to measure.
People who secretly work with the researcher in a study while pretending to be regular participants
The ethical principle that personal information obtained from a participant in research or therapy should not be revealed without the individual's permission.
The post-experimental explanation of a study, including its purpose and any deceptions, to its participants.
Agreement from a minor or someone who cannot legally give full consent to participate in a study after the research has been explained in a way they can understand
The process of giving participants enough information about a study—such as its purpose, procedures, risks, and benefits—so they can voluntarily decide whether or not to participate
A committee that reviews research studies to make sure the study is ethical and protects the rights, safety, and well-being of participants before the research can begin

A type of survey response scale used to measure attitudes or opinions by asking respondents to rate their level of agreement or disagreement with a statement, usually on a range (such as “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree”)
The ethical requirement that researchers ensure participants do not suffer undue physical or psychological harm during the study.
Research that focuses on non-numerical data, such as subjective experiences, feelings, or beliefs.
Research that translates the social world into numbers that can be treated mathematically.
A distribution that has two distinct peaks or most common scores (modes)
Statistical methods used to organize, summarize, and describe data in a meaningful way. This includes measures such as mean, median, mode, range, and standard deviation

A measure of how strong or meaningful a relationship or difference is in a study. Unlike statistical significance, effect size shows the magnitude of the result, helping researchers understand how important the finding is in practical terms
Statistical methods used to make conclusions or predictions about a larger population based on data from a sample
The arithmetic average of a distribution, obtained by adding the scores and then dividing by the number of scores.
A statistical value that represents the center or typical score in a data set. The most common measures are the mean, median, and mode
Statistics that describe how much data values differ or spread out in a data set. Common measures of variation include range and standard deviation
The middle score in a distribution; half the scores are above it and half are below it.
The most frequently occurring score(s) in a distribution.
A distribution in which most scores are clustered on the high end, with a few unusually low scores creating a long tail to the left
A symmetrical, bell-shaped curve that describes the distribution of many types of data; most scores fall near the mean.
The percentage of scores that fall below a specific score in a distribution.
A distribution in which most scores are clustered on the low end, with a few unusually high scores creating a long tail to the right
The difference between the highest and lowest scores in a distribution.
A measure of how spread out data are from the mean (average). A low standard deviation means most scores are close to the mean, while a high standard deviation means the scores are more spread out
A statistical statement of how likely it is that an obtained result occurred by chance (noted by p-value).
The scientific study of observable behavior, and its explanation by principles of learning (e.g., conditioning, reinforcement).
A branch of psychology that links biological (genetic, neural, hormonal) and psychological processes.
An integrated approach that incorporates biological, psychological, and social-cultural levels of analysis.
A psychological approach that focuses on how people think, perceive, remember, and solve problems, emphasizing the role of mental processes in behavior
A perspective that emphasizes the growth potential of healthy people and the individual's potential for personal growth.
A branch of psychology that studies how unconscious drives and conflicts influence behavior, and uses that information to treat people with psychological disorders.
The study of how situations and cultures affect our behavior and thinking.
The controversial practice or advocacy of improving the human species by selectively mating people with specific desirable hereditary traits.
The study of the evolution of behavior and the mind, using principles of natural selection.
An increased likelihood of developing a particular disease or trait based on a person's genetic makeup.
The genetic transfer of characteristics from parents to offspring.
The principle that traits leading to increased reproduction and survival will most likely be passed on to succeeding generations.
The influence of our inherited characteristics (genetics) on personality, physical growth, and social interactions.
The influence of environmental factors such as family, culture, and experience on development.
Research studies that compare identical and fraternal twins to examine the relative influence of genetics and environment on behavior and traits
Identical twins formed when a single fertilized egg splits into two embryos, resulting in twins who share nearly all of the same genetic material
Fraternal twins formed when two separate eggs are fertilized by two different sperm cells, resulting in twins who share about 50% of their genetic material
The molecule that carries the genetic instructions for the development, functioning, and inheritance of traits in living organisms
The study of how environmental factors can influence the expression of genes without changing the underlying DNA sequence
A measure of how much differences in a trait among individuals in a population are due to genetic variation
The division of the peripheral nervous system that automatically regulates involuntary body functions such as heartbeat, breathing, digestion, and gland activity
The division of the nervous system consisting of the brain and spinal cord, which processes information and coordinates the body’s responses
The division of the autonomic nervous system that calms the body and conserves energy by promoting “rest-and-digest” functions after a stressful situation
The sensory and motor neurons that connect the central nervous system to the rest of the body.
The division of the peripheral nervous system that controls the body's skeletal muscles (voluntary movements).
The division of the autonomic nervous system that activates the body’s “fight-or-flight” response during stress or danger, increasing alertness and preparing the body for action
A neurotransmitter that enables communication between neurons and muscles and also plays an important role in learning and memory
A brief electrical impulse that travels down the axon of a neuron, allowing it to transmit information to other neurons, muscles, or glands
Compulsive craving of drugs or certain behaviors (such as gambling) despite known adverse consequences.
A hormone released during stress that increases heart rate, breathing, blood pressure, and energy as part of the body’s fight-or-flight response
Chemicals that bind to and activate receptors, increasing or mimicking the effects of a neurotransmitter
A depressant drug that slows central nervous system activity, impairing judgment, memory, coordination, and reaction time
A neuron’s reaction of either firing (with a full-strength response) or not firing.
Chemicals that bind to receptors and block or reduce the effects of a neurotransmitter
A stimulant drug found in coffee, tea, and soda that increases alertness.
A powerful stimulant drug that increases dopamine levels in the brain by blocking its reuptake, leading to intense feelings of euphoria, energy, and increased alertness
The process during an action potential when a neuron becomes less negative inside due to sodium ions entering the cell, making it more likely to fire an electrical signal
Psychoactive drugs that slow down activity in the central nervous system, reducing arousal, anxiety, and bodily functions such as heart rate and breathing
A neurotransmitter involved in movement, motivation, reward, and pleasure, and linked to disorders such as Parkinson’s disease and schizophrenia
Literally morphine within—natural, opiate-like neurotransmitters linked to pain control and to pleasure.
Neurotransmitters that increase the likelihood that the receiving neuron will fire an action potential
The brain’s primary inhibitory neurotransmitter, which reduces neural activity and helps regulate anxiety, sleep, and muscle tension
A hormone produced mainly in the stomach that stimulates hunger and signals the brain to increase food intake
Cells in the nervous system that support, nourish, and protect neurons
The brain’s primary excitatory neurotransmitter, involved in learning, memory, and neural communication
Psychoactive drugs that alter perception, mood, and thought processes and can cause hallucinations, or sensory experiences that are not based in reality
An opioid drug that is converted into morphine in the brain and produces intense pain relief and euphoria by activating opioid receptors
Chemical messengers that are manufactured by the endocrine glands, travel through the bloodstream, and affect other tissues.
Neurotransmitters that decrease the likelihood that the receiving neuron will fire an action potential
Neurons located in the central nervous system that connect sensory neurons to motor neurons and help process and interpret information
A hormone produced by fat cells that helps regulate hunger and body weight by signaling to the brain that the body has enough stored energy
A mild hallucinogen that can amplify sensitivity to colors, sounds, tastes, and smells, but also relax and disinhibit.
A hormone that helps regulate sleep and the body’s circadian rhythms
Neurons that carry outgoing information from the brain and spinal cord to the muscles and glands (Efferent).
A neurological disease in which the immune system damages the myelin sheath of neurons, disrupting communication between the brain and the rest of the body
An autoimmune disorder in which antibodies block or destroy receptors for acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, leading to muscle weakness and fatigue
Specialized nerve cells that transmit information throughout the body using electrical and chemical signals
A neurotransmitter and hormone involved in alertness, arousal, attention, and the body’s stress response
A class of drugs that reduce pain and produce feelings of pleasure by acting on the brain’s opioid receptors, often by mimicking natural endorphins
A hormone involved in social bonding, trust, childbirth, and breastfeeding
Chemicals that affect the central nervous system and alter mood, perception, consciousness, or behavior by influencing neurotransmitter activity in the brain
The neural pathway that controls a reflex action, involving a sensory neuron, interneuron (in most cases), and motor neuron that produce an automatic, rapid response to a stimulus
A period of inactivity after a neuron has fired, during which it cannot fire again until it resets.
The stable, negative electrical charge of a neuron when it is not firing, maintained by the balance of ions inside and outside the cell
The process by which neurotransmitters are reabsorbed by the sending neuron after transmitting a signal, helping to clear the synapse and regulate signal strength
Chemicals that block the reabsorption of neurotransmitters by the sending neuron, increasing the amount of neurotransmitter available in the synapse
Neurons that carry incoming information from the sensory receptors to the brain and spinal cord (Afferent).
A neurotransmitter involved in mood, sleep, appetite, and emotional regulation, with low levels often linked to depressio
Psychoactive drugs that increase activity in the central nervous system, leading to heightened alertness, energy, and arousal
A neurotransmitter involved in the transmission of pain messages to the brain.
The level of electrical charge a neuron must reach in order to generate an action potential and send a neural signal
The diminishing effect with regular use of the same dose of a drug, requiring the user to take larger and larger doses to experience the effect.
The discomfort and distress that follow discontinuing an addictive drug or behavior.
A structure in the limbic system involved in processing emotions, especially fear and aggression, and in forming emotional memories
A language disorder caused by damage to areas of the brain responsible for language, resulting in difficulties with speaking, understanding, reading, or writing
Areas of the cerebral cortex that are not involved in primary motor or sensory functions; rather, they are involved in higher mental functions.
The part of the brain that connects the brain to the spinal cord and controls basic life-sustaining functions such as breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure
A region of the left frontal lobe that is involved in speech production and language expression; damage to this area can cause difficulty speaking fluently (Broca’s aphasia)
A brain structure located at the back of the brain that coordinates balance, movement, and fine motor skills, and is also involved in motor learning
The outer layer of the brain responsible for higher-level functions such as thinking, perceiving, language, memory, and voluntary movement
The concept that the left hemisphere controls the right side of the body, and the right hemisphere controls the left side.
A thick band of neural fibers that connects the left and right hemispheres of the brain, allowing communication between them
A medical imaging technique that uses X-rays to create detailed cross-sectional images of the brain and other parts of the body
Electroencephalogram; an amplified recording of the waves of electrical activity sweeping across the brain's surface.
Cognitive processes that include working memory, flexible thinking, and self-control.
A brain imaging technique that measures changes in blood flow to show which areas of the brain are active during specific mental task
The part of the cerebral cortex involved in decision-making, planning, reasoning, problem-solving, personality, and voluntary movement
The two halves of the brain (left and right) that specialize in different functions but communicate with each other through the corpus callosum
The tendency of some cognitive functions to be specialized to either the left or right hemisphere.
Complex cognitive processes such as analysis, synthesis, evaluation, and creation.
A structure in the limbic system that is important for forming new memories and helping with learning and spatial navigation
A small brain structure that helps regulate essential body functions such as hunger, thirst, body temperature, and hormone release by controlling the endocrine system
An area of damaged or destroyed tissue in the body or brain, often studied to understand the function of the affected region
A group of brain structures involved in emotion, motivation, and memory, including the hippocampus, amygdala, and parts of the hypothalamus
A part of the brainstem that controls vital involuntary functions such as breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure
An area at the rear of the frontal lobes that controls voluntary movements.
A brain imaging technique that uses magnetic fields and radio waves to produce detailed images of the brain’s structure and other body tissues
The part of the cerebral cortex located at the back of the brain that is primarily responsible for processing visual information
The part of the cerebral cortex that processes sensory information such as touch, temperature, and pain, and helps with spatial awareness and perception
A brain imaging technique that uses a radioactive tracer to measure activity and energy use in different areas of the brain
A small gland often called the “master gland” because it releases hormones that control other endocrine glands and regulate growth, metabolism, and reproduction
The brain’s ability to change and reorganize itself by forming new neural connections in response to learning, experience, or injury
A part of the brainstem that helps regulate sleep, breathing, and arousal and acts as a bridge for communication between different parts of the brain
The forward part of the frontal lobes responsible for judgment, planning, and processing new memories.
A network of neurons in the brainstem that regulates alertness, attention, and sleep-wake cycles by filtering incoming sensory information
A group of brain structures, including areas of the limbic system, that are activated by pleasurable experiences and reinforce behaviors through dopamine release
Area at the front of the parietal lobes that registers and processes body touch and movement sensations

Studies of individuals whose corpus callosum has been severed to reduce severe epilepsy, showing how the left and right hemispheres of the brain can function independently and specialize in different tasks
The part of the cerebral cortex involved in processing auditory information, language comprehension, and memory
A brain structure that acts as the brain’s main relay station, receiving sensory information and sending it to the appropriate areas of the cerebral cortex for processing
A region of the left temporal lobe involved in language comprehension; damage to this area can result in fluent but meaningless speech and difficulty understanding language (Wernicke’s aphasia)
The theory that dreams are the brain's attempt to make sense of random neural activity occurring during sleep.
Relatively slow brain waves that are most common when a person is awake but relaxed and calm, often occurring just before falling asleep
The body’s internal biological clock that regulates the sleep-wake cycle and other physiological processes on a roughly 24-hour schedule
A person’s awareness of themselves and their environment, including thoughts, feelings, sensations, and perceptions at any given moment
The theory that sleep, especially REM and deep NREM sleep, helps stabilize and strengthen newly formed memories so they can be stored long-term
Very slow, high-amplitude brain waves that occur primarily during deep NREM Stage 3 sleep
Vivid, dreamlike experiences (such as falling or seeing flashes of light) that occur during the transition from wakefulness to sleep, especially in NREM Stage 1
A sleep disorder characterized by persistent difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or getting restful sleep despite adequate opportunity to do so
Fatigue and sleep disturbance resulting from disruption of the body's normal circadian rhythm following long flights through different time zones.
A sleep disorder characterized by sudden, uncontrollable sleep attacks during waking hours, often including rapid entry into REM sleep and possible loss of muscle control
A sleep disorder involving sudden episodes of intense fear, screaming, and high arousal during deep NREM sleep, typically with little to no recall of the event upon waking
A very light sleep stage that occurs as a transition from wakefulness to sleep, marked by slowed brain activity, muscle relaxation, and brief hypnagogic sensations
A deeper stage of light sleep characterized by slower heart rate and body temperature, with brain activity showing sleep spindles
The deepest stage of non-REM sleep, characterized by delta waves and important for physical restoration, growth, and recovery
An increase in REM sleep that occurs after a person is deprived of REM sleep, causing the body to spend more time in REM during subsequent sleep cycles
A stage of sleep marked by rapid eye movements, vivid dreaming, high brain activity, and temporary muscle paralysis
A sleep disorder in which the normal muscle paralysis of REM sleep is absent, causing a person to physically act out their dreams, sometimes violently
The theory that sleep serves to repair and rejuvenate the body and brain, helping restore energy, support growth, and maintain overall physical and mental functioning
Work schedules that take place outside the traditional 9-to-5 day, often disrupting circadian rhythms and sleep patterns.
A naturally recurring state of rest characterized by reduced consciousness, slowed bodily functions, and brain activity that supports restoration, memory consolidation, and overall health
A sleep disorder characterized by temporary cessations of breathing during sleep and repeated momentary awakenings.
Brief bursts of rapid brain activity that occur during NREM Stage 2 sleep and are believed to play a role in memory consolidation and protecting sleep from external disturbances
A sleep disorder in which a person walks or performs other complex behaviors while still asleep, usually during deep NREM Stage 3 sleep, with little or no memory of the event
Slow brain waves that are typically seen during light sleep (especially NREM Stage 1 and 2) and are also associated with deep relaxation and early stages of sleep
The minimum stimulus energy needed to detect a particular stimulus 50 percent of the time.
The process by which the eye's lens changes shape to focus near or far objects on the retina.
Visual sensations that continue after the original stimulus is removed, often appearing in complementary colors due to fatigue in opponent-process color receptors
The height of a light wave, which determines the intensity or brightness of the light
The height or intensity of a sound wave, which determines the loudness of the sound
A membrane in the cochlea that vibrates in response to sound waves and stimulates hair cells to help convert sound into neural signals
The point at which the optic nerve leaves the eye where there are no receptor cells
A condition in which a person can respond to a visual stimulus without consciously experiencing it.
Neurons in the retina that receive signals from rods and cones and transmit visual information to ganglion cells
A fluid-filled, snail-shaped structure in the inner ear that converts sound vibrations into neural signals for the brain
Hearing loss caused by damage to the mechanical system that conducts sound waves to the cochlea
Photoreceptor cells in the retina responsible for color vision and fine detail, functioning best in bright light
The transparent, curved outer layer of the eye that helps focus incoming light onto the retina and protects the eye
A form of color blindness in which only two of the three primary colors can be perceived.
A condition in which faraway objects are seen more clearly than near objects because the image of near objects is focused behind the retina.
A small central area of the retina with the highest concentration of cones, responsible for sharp central vision and detailed color perception
The theory that the rate of nerve impulses traveling up the auditory nerve matches the frequency of a tone, thus enabling us to sense its pitch.
Neurons in the retina that receive signals from bipolar cells and transmit visual information from the eye to the brain through the optic nerve
The theory that pain is experienced when pain signals pass through a “gate” in the spinal cord, which can be opened or closed by other sensory input or signals from the brain
The sense of taste, which allows the detection of chemical substances in food through taste receptor cells on the tongue
Sensory receptor cells in the cochlea that detect sound vibrations and convert them into neural impulses sent to the brain
The colored part of the eye that controls the size of the pupil and regulates the amount of light entering the eye
The minimum difference between two stimuli required for detection 50 percent of the time
The sense that provides awareness of the position and movement of body parts through receptors in muscles, tendons, and joints
The transparent structure behind the pupil that changes shape to help focus images on the retina.
Individuals with an average number of taste buds and typical sensitivity to basic tastes, falling between supertasters and non-tasters
A rare form of color blindness in which a person sees only shades of one color or only black, white, and gray because of absent or nonfunctioning cone cells
A condition in which nearby objects are seen more clearly than distant objects because distant objects focus in front of the retina.
Individuals who have a relatively low number of taste buds, making them less sensitive to certain tastes, especially bitter flavors
The sense of smell, which detects airborne chemical molecules through receptors in the nose and sends signals to the brain for interpretation
The theory that color vision is controlled by opposing pairs of color receptors (red-green, blue-yellow, black-white), where activation of one color in the pair inhibits the other
The nerve that carries visual information from the retina to the brain for processing
A condition in which a person feels sensations, including pain, in a limb that has been amputated, due to continued brain representation of the missing limb
Chemical signals released by an animal that communicate information and affect the behavior of other animals of the same species.
The theory that links the pitch we hear with the location where the cochlea's membrane is stimulated
A neurological condition, often called “face blindness,” in which a person has difficulty recognizing or distinguishing faces despite normal vision
The adjustable opening in the center of the iris that controls how much light enters the eye
The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye that contains photoreceptor cells (rods and cones) and converts light into neural signals sent to the brain
Photoreceptor cells in the retina that are highly sensitive to light and allow for vision in low-light conditions, but do not detect color
Three fluid-filled canals in the inner ear that help maintain balance by detecting rotation.
The process by which our sensory receptors and nervous system receive and represent stimulus energies from our environment.
A type of hearing loss caused by damage to the inner ear (cochlea) or auditory nerve, often resulting in permanent impairment of sound transmission to the brain
The diminished sensitivity to a constant or unchanging stimulus over time, allowing the brain to focus on more important changes in the environment
The principle that one sense may influence another, as when the smell of food influences its taste
The principle that different senses can influence and enhance one another, such as how smell and taste work together to create flavor perception
The ability to identify the origin or direction of a sound by using differences in timing and intensity of the sound reaching each ear
Individuals who have a higher-than-average number of taste buds, making them especially sensitive to certain tastes, particularly bitter flavors
A perceptual phenomenon in which stimulation of one sensory or cognitive pathway leads to involuntary experiences in another, such as seeing colors when hearing music
The sense that allows the body to perceive pressure, temperature, pain, and body position through sensory receptors in the skin and other tissues
The process by which sensory receptors convert physical energy from the environment (such as light, sound, or pressure) into neural signals that the brain can interpret
The theory that color vision is based on three types of cones in the retina that are sensitive to red, green, and blue light, with all other colors created by combinations of these signals
The sensory system in the inner ear that helps maintain balance and posture by detecting changes in head movement and spatial orientation
The theory that groups of auditory neurons fire in rapid succession to help transmit sounds, especially for higher-frequency sounds that individual neurons cannot fire fast enough to encode alone
The distance between successive peaks of a sound wave, which is related to the sound’s frequency and perceived pitch
The distance between successive peaks of a light wave, which determines the perceived color of light

The principle that the just noticeable difference between two stimuli is a constant proportion of the original stimulus intensity, meaning larger stimuli require a greater change to detect a difference
The cognitive process of focusing awareness on specific stimuli or information while ignoring other competing stimuli
A perceptual illusion in which a stationary point of light in a dark or featureless environment appears to move due to lack of visual reference points
Depth cues that require the use of both eyes, such as retinal disparity and convergence, to help perceive distance and depth
A type of perceptual processing that starts with sensory input and builds up to a complete perception based on incoming data from the environment
A perceptual phenomenon in which people fail to notice significant changes in a visual scene when their attention is not focused on those changes
A Gestalt principle of perception in which the brain fills in missing parts of a visual image to perceive it as a complete whole
The ability to focus one’s attention on a single conversation in a noisy environment while still being able to notice personally relevant information, such as one’s name
The surrounding information, situation, or environment that influences how sensory input is interpreted and perceived
A binocular depth cue in which the eyes turn inward to focus on a nearby object, with greater eye muscle strain indicating closer distance
A Gestalt principle of perception in which the brain organizes visual information by separating a focal object (figure) from its background (ground)
A school of psychology that emphasizes how people naturally organize sensory information into meaningful wholes rather than separate parts
A failure to notice a fully visible but unexpected stimulus because attention is focused on something else
A monocular depth cue in which one object partially blocking another object is perceived as being closer
A monocular depth cue in which parallel lines appear to converge as they move farther into the distance, helping create the perception of depth
Depth cues that can be perceived with one eye alone, helping the brain judge distance and depth in a visual scene
The tendency to perceive objects as stable and unchanging (in size, shape, color, or brightness) even when sensory information changes
A mental predisposition or expectation that influences how we perceive and interpret sensory information
An illusion of movement created when two or more lights close to each other blink on and off in succession, causing the perception of motion between them
A Gestalt principle of perception in which objects that are close together are perceived as belonging to the same group
A monocular depth cue in which clearer, sharper objects are perceived as closer than hazy or blurry objects
A monocular depth cue in which smaller retinal images are perceived as farther away and larger retinal images as closer, assuming the objects are similar in actual size
A binocular depth cue based on the slight difference between the images seen by each eye, which the brain uses to perceive depth
Mental frameworks or cognitive structures that help organize and interpret information based on past experiences and knowledge
The ability to focus on one specific stimulus while filtering out other distractions in the environment
A Gestalt principle of perception in which objects that are similar in appearance are perceived as belonging together or forming a group
The illusion of continuous movement created when a series of slightly different still images are shown rapidly in succession, as in movies or animation
A monocular depth cue in which coarse, detailed textures appear closer, while smoother, less detailed textures appear farther away
A type of perceptual processing that uses prior knowledge, expectations, and experience to interpret and make sense of sensory information
The process of modifying existing schemas or creating new ones in response to new information that does not fit into current understanding
Step-by-step, logical procedures or rules that guarantee a solution to a problem if followed correctly
The cognitive process of incorporating new information into existing schemas without changing the original framework
A mental shortcut where people estimate the likelihood of events based on how easily examples come to mind, often influenced by recent, vivid, or memorable information
Mental categories or groupings of similar objects, ideas, or events that help the brain organize information and make sense of the world
A type of thinking that focuses on finding a single correct answer or solution to a problem by narrowing down possibilities
The ability to produce original and valuable ideas or solutions by thinking in novel and flexible ways
A type of thinking that generates multiple possible solutions or ideas by exploring many different directions and possibilities
The way information is presented or “framed,” which can influence how people perceive and respond to it, even when the underlying information is the same
A cognitive bias that limits a person to using an object only in its traditional or familiar way, making it harder to see alternative uses in problem-solving
The mistaken belief that past random events influence future independent events, such as thinking a coin is “due” to land on heads after several tails in a row
Simple, efficient mental shortcuts or “rules of thumb” that speed up decision-making and problem-solving, though they may sometimes lead to errors
A tendency to approach problems using strategies or solutions that have worked in the past, which can sometimes hinder finding new or better solutions
The activation of specific associations in memory before carrying out a task, which can influence perception, thinking, or behavior without conscious awareness
The most typical or best example of a concept that helps people quickly recognize and classify new objects or ideas
A mental shortcut where people estimate the likelihood of an event based on how easily examples come to mind, often influenced by recent or memorable experiences
The tendency to continue an endeavor because of previously invested time, money, or effort, even when future costs outweigh the benefits
The unconscious and effortless processing of information, such as reading familiar words or walking, that requires little attention or awareness
The component of working memory that directs attention, manages cognitive tasks, and coordinates information from other parts of working memory.
The process of encoding information by focusing on its meaning and associations, leading to stronger and longer-lasting memories.
A brief sensory memory system that stores auditory information for a few seconds after a sound is heard.
The encoding of information that requires conscious attention and deliberate effort, such as studying vocabulary or memorizing facts.
The process of converting sensory input into a form that can be stored and later retrieved from memory.
A type of long-term memory that involves the conscious recollection of personal experiences and specific events, including time and place details.
Memory of facts and experiences that can be consciously recalled and described, including episodic and semantic memory.
A brief sensory memory system that holds visual information for a fraction of a second after the stimulus is gone.
A type of long-term memory that operates without conscious awareness, influencing skills, habits, and learned behaviors (like tying your shoes or typing).
A model of memory that compares the mind to a computer, describing memory as a process of encoding, storing, and retrieving information.
A theory of memory that proposes that the depth at which information is processed (from shallow to deep/meaningful processing) determines how well it is remembered.
The relatively permanent storage of information, experiences, and skills that can last from minutes to a lifetime and has a virtually unlimited capacity.
A long-lasting increase in the strength of synaptic connections between neurons that occurs with repeated activation and is believed to be a neural basis for learning and memory.

A theory proposing that memory consists of three separate stores—sensory memory, short-term memory, and long-term memory—with information flowing through them through processes like attention and rehearsal.
A component of working memory that temporarily stores and rehearses verbal and auditory information, such as spoken words or sounds.
A type of implicit long-term memory that stores information about how to perform tasks and skills, such as riding a bike or typing, often without conscious awareness.
Memory for remembering to perform an intended action in the future, such as remembering to take medication or attend an appointment.
The process of accessing and bringing stored information from long-term memory into conscious awareness.
Semantic Memory – A type of long-term memory that stores general knowledge, facts, concepts, and meanings about the world, independent of personal experience.
Sensory Memory – The very brief storage of sensory information (such as sights or sounds) that lasts only a fraction of a second to a few seconds before it is either processed further or forgotten.
The process of encoding information based on superficial features such as appearance or sound, rather than meaning, which typically leads to weaker memory retention.
The temporary storage of a small amount of information that is available for immediate use and lasts only a short time without rehearsal.
The stage of memory in which encoded information is held and preserved in the brain over time.
The process of encoding information based on its physical appearance or visual features, such as shape, color, or format, rather than meaning or sound.
The process of encoding information based on how words sound, focusing on their auditory qualities rather than meaning.
The process of encoding information based on its meaning and understanding, which leads to stronger and more durable memories.
A component of working memory that temporarily stores and manipulates visual and spatial information, such as images, shapes, and location in space.
A limited-capacity memory system that temporarily holds and actively processes information needed for tasks such as learning, reasoning, and problem-solving
Mental groupings used to organize objects, ideas, or experiences based on shared features or characteristics.
A memory strategy that involves grouping individual pieces of information into larger, more meaningful units to improve short-term memory capacity and recall.
A learning strategy in which study sessions are spread out over time, leading to better long-term retention compared to massed practice (cramming).
Systems of organization in which information is arranged in levels, from broad general concepts to more specific subcategories, to help structure and simplify understanding.
A learning strategy that involves studying information in a single, long session (cramming), which often leads to weaker long-term retention compared to spaced practice.
The process of stabilizing and strengthening a memory after it is first formed, often involving the transfer of information from short-term to long-term memory, especially during sleep.
A mnemonic device that improves memory by associating information with specific locations in a familiar place, mentally “walking through” those locations to recall the items.
Memory aids or techniques that help improve recall by organizing information in more meaningful or easily remembered ways, such as acronyms, rhymes, or imagery.
The tendency to better remember items at the beginning of a list because they receive more attention and rehearsal.
The tendency to better remember the last items in a list because they are still present in short-term memory.
A memory phenomenon in which people are more likely to remember items at the beginning and end of a list than those in the middle.
The tendency for information to be better remembered when study sessions are spaced out over time rather than crammed into a single session.
A progressive neurological disorder that causes gradual memory loss, impaired thinking, and changes in behavior due to brain degeneration, especially in areas involved in memory and cognition.
A type of memory loss in which a person is unable to form new long-term memories after the event that caused the amnesia, while older memories remain intact.
Memory for personal life events and knowledge about oneself, combining factual details and emotional experiences that help form one’s identity.
A memory strategy that involves actively thinking about the meaning of new information and connecting it to existing knowledge to improve long-term retention.
A rare condition in which a person can recall an extremely detailed and accurate account of nearly every day of their life, often without conscious effort.
The inability of adults to remember early childhood experiences, typically before age 3 or 4, due to the ongoing development of brain structures involved in memory.
A memory strategy that involves repeatedly reviewing information (such as silently repeating it) to keep it in short-term memory without necessarily encoding its meaning.
A type of memory loss in which a person is unable to recall events that occurred before the injury or incident that caused the amnesia, while the ability to form new memories may remain intact.
The tendency to better recall information when the external environment during retrieval matches the environment in which the information was originally learned.
Awareness and understanding of one’s own thought processes, including the ability to monitor, evaluate, and regulate learning and problem-solving strategies.
The tendency to recall memories that match one’s current emotional state, such as remembering sad events more easily when feeling sad.
A memory task that requires generating previously learned information from memory, such as answering an essay question without hints or choices.
A memory process that involves identifying previously learned information when it is presented again, often with the help of cues (such as multiple-choice answers).
Stimuli or hints that help trigger the process of retrieving information from long-term memory.
The process of actively recalling information from memory, which strengthens long-term retention and makes future recall easier.
The tendency to better recall information when a person is in the same internal state (mood, emotional state, or physiological condition) as when the information was learned.
The finding that actively testing oneself on material improves long-term memory more than simply re-studying the information.
The idea that memory is not a perfect recording of events, but is actively built and reconstructed using stored information, expectations, and prior knowledge.
A failure to process information into long-term memory, meaning it was never properly stored in the first place.
A graph showing how quickly information is forgotten over time when it is not reinforced, with the steepest loss occurring soon after learning.
The tendency for imagined events to be remembered as real, or for confidence in false memories to increase after repeatedly imagining them.
The tendency for post-event information to distort or change a person’s memory of an original event.
When older memories interfere with the recall of newer information.
The unconscious blocking of painful or anxiety-producing memories from conscious awareness.
When newer information interferes with the recall of older memories.
The process in which a retrieved memory is modified before being stored again, resulting in a change of the original memory
The inability to remember where, when, or how a memory was learned, even though the information itself is remembered.
The temporary inability to retrieve a known word or memory, accompanied by the feeling that retrieval is imminent.
Tests that measure what a person has already learned in a specific subject or area.
Tests designed to predict a person’s future ability to learn or perform certain tasks.
The actual age of a person measured in years, months, and days since birth.
The extent to which a test accurately measures the psychological concept it is intended to measure.
The ability to use learned knowledge and experience, such as vocabulary and general information.
A statistical method used to identify clusters of related test items that measure underlying abilities or traits.
The belief that intelligence and abilities are static and cannot be significantly changed.
The ability to solve new problems, think abstractly, and adapt to novel situations.
The observed rise in average IQ scores over time across generations.
A proposed general mental ability that underlies performance on a wide variety of cognitive tasks.
The belief that intelligence and abilities can be developed through effort, learning, and persistence.
The ability to learn from experience, reason, solve problems, and adapt to new situations.
A score derived from standardized tests that is intended to measure general intelligence relative to others.
The level of cognitive performance typical of a certain age group, based on test performance.
The process of establishing test standards by comparing scores from a representative sample population.
A score indicating the percentage of people who scored at or below a particular score on a test.
The extent to which a test accurately predicts future performance or outcomes.
The consistency of a test in producing stable and repeatable results over time.
A measure of reliability in which a test is divided into two halves and scores on both halves are compared.
The process of administering and scoring a test in a consistent way for all test takers.
Performance improvement that occurs when positive stereotypes about a group enhance confidence and outcomes.
The risk of underperformance when individuals are aware of negative stereotypes about their group.
The consistency of test scores when the same test is given to the same people at different times.
The extent to which a test measures what it is intended to measure.
Development that occurs gradually and smoothly over time, with small incremental changes rather than distinct stages.
Development that occurs in distinct stages, with clear shifts or changes between phases of growth.
The influence of genetic inheritance and biology on development and behavior.
The influence of environmental factors, such as experience, culture, and learning, on development and behavior.
Research studies that compare individuals of different ages at one point in time to examine developmental differences.
Research studies that follow the same individuals over a long period of time to observe changes in development.

Specific windows of time in development during which an organism is especially sensitive to certain environmental influences, and certain abilities or traits must develop for normal development to occur.
A condition caused by prenatal alcohol exposure that can lead to physical abnormalities, cognitive impairments, and behavioral problems in a developing fetus.
The ability to use small muscle movements, especially in the hands and fingers, to perform precise tasks such as writing, buttoning clothing, or using utensils.
The ability to use large muscle groups to perform broad physical movements such as walking, running, jumping, and balancing.
A rapid period of physical growth in height and weight, typically occurring during puberty.
A rapid, innate form of learning that occurs during a critical period in early development, in which young animals form strong attachments to the first moving object they see (often a parent).
The natural, biologically driven process of physical and cognitive development that unfolds over time, largely independent of experience or practice.
The first occurrence of menstruation, marking the onset of female reproductive capability during puberty.
The natural biological stage in a woman’s life when menstrual cycles permanently stop, typically occurring in middle adulthood, marking the end of fertility.
The reproductive organs and structures directly involved in reproduction, such as the ovaries, testes, uterus, and external genitalia, that develop and mature during puberty.
The developmental stage during which a person’s body undergoes physical changes and sexual maturation, becoming capable of reproduction due to hormonal changes.
Inborn, automatic responses to specific stimuli that help protect the body and support survival, such as blinking or withdrawing a hand from a hot surface.
An infant reflex in which touching or stroking the cheek causes the baby to turn their head and begin searching for a nipple to help with feeding.
Physical traits that develop during puberty but are not directly involved in reproduction, such as breast development, voice deepening, and body hair growth.
Developmental windows of time when the brain is especially responsive to certain experiences, making learning easier, though not absolutely required for development to occur.
The first ejaculation of sperm in males, marking the onset of sexual maturity and reproductive capability during puberty.
Harmful substances or environmental agents that can cause birth defects or developmental abnormalities during prenatal development, such as alcohol, certain drugs, or infections.
A laboratory setup used to test depth perception in infants and young animals, where a glass surface creates the illusion of a drop-off to measure responses to perceived height and danger.
The ability to think about concepts that are not physically present or directly experienced, such as ideas, possibilities, symbols, and hypothetical situations.
The process of modifying existing schemas or creating new ones in response to new information that does not fit into current understanding
The belief, common in early childhood, that inanimate objects have thoughts, feelings, or intentions (e.g., “the toy is sad”).
The cognitive process of incorporating new information into existing schemas without changing the original framework

Piaget’s third stage of cognitive development (about ages 7–11) in which children develop logical thinking about concrete events, understand conservation, and can perform mental operations on real, tangible objects.
The understanding that certain properties of objects (such as volume, mass, or number) remain the same even when their appearance or arrangement changes.
The ability to use learned knowledge and experience, such as vocabulary and general information.
A broad category of brain disorders characterized by a gradual decline in memory, thinking, reasoning, and daily functioning that is severe enough to interfere with everyday life.
The inability to see things from another person’s perspective, often seen in young children who assume others think and perceive the world the same way they do.
The ability to solve new problems, think abstractly, and adapt to novel situations.

Piaget’s fourth stage of cognitive development (about age 12 and up) in which individuals develop the ability to think abstractly, reason logically about hypothetical situations, and use systematic problem-solving.
The ability to consider possible outcomes, situations, or “what if” scenarios without needing direct experience or concrete evidence.
Internal representations (such as images, words, or concepts) that the mind uses to stand for objects, ideas, or experiences in the environment.
In Vygotsky’s theory, a person who has a higher level of knowledge or skill in a particular task than the learner, such as a teacher, peer, or expert, who can provide guidance and support.
The understanding that objects continue to exist even when they cannot be seen, heard, or directly sensed.

Piaget’s second stage of cognitive development (about ages 2–7) in which children use language and symbols to represent the world but think in a more intuitive and egocentric way, lacking logical operations.
A form of play in which children use imagination to act out roles or scenarios, using objects or actions to represent something else (e.g., pretending a stick is a sword).
The ability to mentally reverse an action or process, understanding that objects or operations can be changed and then returned to their original state.
Temporary support and guidance provided by a teacher, peer, or adult that helps a learner complete a task they could not do alone, with support slowly removed as the learner becomes more capable.
A mental framework or concept that helps organize and interpret information based on past experiences.
Piaget’s first stage of cognitive development (birth to about age 2) in which infants learn about the world through their senses and actions, and develop object permanence.
The ability to understand that other people have their own thoughts, beliefs, intentions, and perspectives that may differ from one’s own.
In Vygotsky’s theory, the range of tasks that a learner can perform with guidance from a more knowledgeable other but cannot yet perform independently.
A stage of early language development in which infants (around 4–10 months) begin producing repetitive consonant-vowel sounds like “ba-ba” or “da-da,” practicing speech-like sounds.
An early stage of language development in infants (around 2–4 months) characterized by soft, vowel-like sounds such as “oo” and “ah,” often reflecting pleasure and comfort.
The set of rules in a language that governs how words are structured and combined to form meaningful sentences, including syntax and word usage.
The smallest units of meaning in a language, including whole words or parts of words (like prefixes and suffixes) that carry meaning, such as “un-” or “-ed.”
A stage of language development in which children use single words to express complete ideas or sentences, such as saying “milk” to mean “I want milk.”
A language learning error in which children apply grammatical rules too broadly, such as saying “goed” instead of “went” or “mouses” instead of “mice.”
The smallest units of sound in a language that can be combined to form words and can change meaning when altered (e.g., changing the “b” in “bat” to “c” creates “cat”).
The part of language that deals with meaning, including how words and sentences convey ideas and how context affects interpretation.
The set of rules that governs the order and arrangement of words in a sentence to create meaningful and grammatically correct statements.
Early language use (around age 2) in which children speak in short, simple sentences that include only essential words, usually nouns and verbs (e.g., “want cookie” instead of “I want a cookie”).
Marcia's identity status where an individual has explored alternatives and committed to a set of values/goals.
Potentially traumatic events that occur in childhood (0-17 years) that can have lasting effects on health and well-being.
A style where the child is distressed when the caregiver leaves and remains distressed or angry upon their return.
The expectations people develop about relationships with others, based on the relationship they had with their primary caregiver.
A restrictive, punitive style of parenting in which parents exhort the child to follow their directions and respect their work and effort.
A parenting style that encourages children to be independent but still places limits and controls on their actions.
Erikson's second stage (1-3 yrs): Toddlers learn to exercise their will and do things for themselves, or they doubt their abilities.
Infants who seem unresponsive to the parent when they are present and are usually not distressed when she leaves.
The dimension of time in relation to a person's development, including life transitions and historical events.
Marcia's identity status where an individual has not yet explored or committed to an identity.
A type of attachment that is marked by an infant's inconsistent or confused reactions to the caregiver's departure and return.
Bronfenbrenner's model which views the person as developing within a complex system of relationships affected by multiple levels of the surrounding environment.
A period from the late teens to mid-twenties, bridging the gap between adolescent dependence and full adult independence and responsibility.
Social settings that a person may not experience firsthand but that still influence development (e.g., a parent's workplace).
Marcia's identity status where an individual has committed to an identity without exploring alternatives (often following parents' lead).
Erikson's seventh stage (middle adulthood): People discover a sense of contributing to the world, or they may feel a lack of purpose.
Erikson's fifth stage (adolescence): Teenagers work at refining a sense of self by testing roles, or they become confused about who they are.
Adolescents' belief that others are as interested in them as they itself are; the feeling of being on stage.
Erikson's fourth stage (6-puberty): Children learn the pleasure of applying themselves to tasks, or they feel inferior.
Erikson's third stage (3-6 yrs): Preschoolers learn to initiate tasks and carry out plans, or they feel guilty about their efforts to be independent.
Attachments marked by anxiety or ambivalence; infants are less likely to explore and may cling to or avoid the caregiver.
Erikson's eighth stage (late adulthood): Reflecting on one's life, an older adult may feel a sense of satisfaction or failure.
Erikson's sixth stage (young adulthood): Individuals form close relationships and gain the capacity for intimate love, or they feel socially isolated.
The larger cultural context, including values, laws, and resources.
The connections between various microsystems (e.g., the relationship between a child's parents and their teacher).
The immediate environment that an individual interacts with directly (e.g., family, school).
Marcia's identity status where an individual is currently exploring alternatives but has not yet made a commitment.
Activity in which children play side by side without interacting.
A style of parenting in which parents are very involved with their children but place few demands or controls on them.
The part of adolescent egocentrism that involves an adolescent's sense of uniqueness and invincibility.
A relationship in which an infant obtains both comfort and confidence from the presence of his or her caregiver.
Emotional distress seen in many infants when they are separated from people with whom they have formed an attachment.
The culturally preferred timing of social events such as marriage, parenthood, and retirement.
A comprehensive theory consisting of eight stages of psychosocial development, each characterized by a specific crisis.
A person's characteristic emotional reactivity and intensity.
Erikson's first stage (0-1 yr): If needs are dependably met, infants develop a sense of basic trust.
The initial stage in classical conditioning; the phase associating a neutral stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus.
The process by which we learn that certain events occur together.
Learning that certain events occur together. The events may be two stimuli (classical) or a response and its consequences (operant).
The psychological view that emphasizes the power of environmental forces on behavior (learning through conditioning).
A propensity for learning particular kinds of associations over others (e.g., taste and nausea).
A type of learning in which one learns to link two or more stimuli and anticipate events.
The learned response to a previously neutral (but now conditioned) stimulus.
An originally irrelevant stimulus that, after association with an unconditioned stimulus, comes to trigger a conditioned response.
A behavior therapy procedure that uses classical conditioning to evoke new responses to stimuli that are triggering unwanted behaviors.
The diminishing of a conditioned response; occurs when a UCS does not follow a CS.
Decreasing responsiveness with repeated stimulation.
A procedure in which the conditioned stimulus in one conditioning experience is paired with a new neutral stimulus, creating a second (often weaker) conditioned stimulus.
The reappearance, after a pause, of an extinguished conditioned response.
The learned ability to distinguish between a conditioned stimulus and stimuli that do not signal an unconditioned stimulus.
The tendency, once a response has been conditioned, for stimuli similar to the conditioned stimulus to elicit similar responses.
A classically conditioned avoidance of a particular food that develops when an organism becomes ill after eating it.
The unlearned, naturally occurring response to the unconditioned stimulus.
A stimulus that naturally and automatically triggers a response.
Reinforcing the desired response every time it occurs.
A reinforcement schedule that reinforces a response only after a specified time has elapsed.
A reinforcement schedule that reinforces a response only after a specified number of responses.
The tendency of learned behavior to gradually revert to biologically predisposed patterns.
Thorndike's principle that behaviors followed by favorable consequences become more likely, and behaviors followed by unfavorable consequences become less likely.
The hopelessness and passive resignation an animal or human learns when unable to avoid repeated aversive events.
Increasing behaviors by stopping or reducing negative stimuli, such as shock. (It is NOT punishment).
A type of learning in which behavior is strengthened if followed by a reinforcer or diminished if followed by a punishment.
Reinforcing a response only part of the time; results in slower acquisition but greater resistance to extinction.
Increasing behaviors by presenting positive stimuli, such as food.
An innately reinforcing stimulus, such as one that satisfies a biological need (e.g., food).
An event that tends to decrease the behavior that it follows.
Any event that strengthens the behavior it follows.
A stimulus that gains its reinforcing power through its association with a primary reinforcer (e.g., money).
An operant conditioning procedure in which reinforcers guide behavior toward closer and closer approximations of the desired behavior.
A reinforcement schedule that reinforces a response at unpredictable time intervals.
A reinforcement schedule that reinforces a response after an unpredictable number of responses.
A mental representation of the layout of one's environment.
A sudden realization of a problem's solution; Aha! moment.
Learning that occurs but is not apparent until there is an incentive to demonstrate it.
The process of observing and imitating a specific behavior.
The theory that we learn social behavior by observing and imitating and by being rewarded or punished (Bandura).
A type of learning that occurs by observing the consequences of another person's behavior
The tendency to attribute our own actions to external causes while attributing others' actions to internal ones.
The process of explaining the causes of behavior and events.
Explaining behavior based on internal factors like personality, character, or ability.
Comparing ourselves to those we perceive as worse off to boost self-esteem.
A person's characteristic way of explaining negative and positive events.
The belief that outcomes are determined by fate, luck, or outside forces.
Overestimating dispositional factors and underestimating situational factors when judging others.
The belief that one has personal control over their life and outcomes.
Repeated exposure to a stimulus increases our preference for it.
Attributing failures to external, unstable, and specific causes.
Attributing failures to internal, stable, and global causes.
The perception that we are worse off than the people we compare ourselves to.
A prediction that causes itself to become true due to the behavior of the believer.
Attributing personal successes to internal factors and failures to external factors.
Explaining behavior based on external factors like environment or social pressure.
Evaluating one's own abilities or opinions by comparing them to others.
Comparing ourselves to those we perceive as better off to motivate ourselves or feel inferior.
Clinging to one's initial beliefs even after they have been discredited.
The tension experienced when our attitudes and behaviors do not match.
The total amount of mental effort being used in working memory.
Searching for information that supports our preconceptions and ignoring contradictory evidence.
Unjustifiable negative behavior toward a group and its members.
The belief that one's own culture or ethnic group is superior.
Unconscious evaluations or feelings toward objects or people.
The tendency to favor our own group over others.
The tendency to believe the world is fair and people get what they deserve.
Viewing members of an out-group as all the same compared to in-group diversity.
An unjustifiable and usually negative attitude toward a group and its members.
A generalized belief about a group of people.
Unselfish concern for the welfare of others.
Factors that determine which parts of a situation a person focuses on.
Physical, mental, and emotional exhaustion caused by prolonged stress.
The finding that a person is less likely to help when others are present.
Persuasion focusing on logic, facts, and the content of the message.
Prioritizing group goals and identity over personal ones.
Adjusting behavior or thinking to match a group standard.
The loss of self-awareness and self-restraint in anonymous group situations.
Feeling less responsible for taking action when others are present.
Following an initial large, rejected request with a smaller, more reasonable one.
Overestimating the degree to which others share our beliefs and behaviors.
Getting someone to agree to a large request by first getting them to agree to a small one.
The tendency for a group's existing beliefs to strengthen after discussion.
When the desire for group harmony overrides realistic appraisal of alternatives.
When our overall positive impression of a person influences our feelings about their specific traits.
Prioritizing personal goals and identity over group goals.
Psychologists who apply psychological principles to the workplace.
Conforming because we believe others have more accurate information.
The presence of several distinct cultural groups within a society.
Conforming to gain approval or avoid being disliked by a group.
Changing behavior in response to a direct order from an authority figure.
Persuasion based on incidental cues like attractiveness or celebrity endorsement.
Any action intended to help others.
Environmental factors that influence how a person reacts in a social setting.
The feeling of being obligated to return a favor or service.
Improved performance on simple or well-learned tasks when others are watching.
The study of how individuals' thoughts and behaviors are influenced by others.
Exerting less effort when working in a group than when working alone.
Understood rules for accepted and expected behavior in a group.
The expectation that people will help those who have helped them.
The expectation that people will help those who are dependent on them.
Situations where individuals' self-interest leads to mutually destructive behavior.
Shared goals that override differences and require cooperation.
Refusing to believe or even perceive painful realities.
Shifting aggressive impulses toward a less threatening object or person.
Unconscious tactics that reduce anxiety by distorting reality.
Focuses on personal growth, free will, and self-actualization.
Information that is not currently conscious but can be easily recalled.
Attributing one's own threatening impulses to others.
Personality tests using ambiguous stimuli to reveal inner dynamics.
Focuses on the unconscious mind and childhood experiences in shaping personality.
Creating self-justifying explanations to hide real reasons for actions.
Switching unacceptable impulses into their opposites.
Retreating to a more infantile or comfortable stage of development.
Banishing anxiety-arousing thoughts and memories from consciousness.
The innate drive to maintain and enhance the human organism.
Channeling unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable activities.
Total acceptance toward another person.
A reservoir of mostly unacceptable thoughts, wishes, and feelings.
Mental activities below the level of conscious awareness that influence behavior.
Trait characterized by being cooperative, trustworthy, and good-natured.
A model consisting of Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism.
Trait characterized by organization, responsibility, and discipline.
The degree to which one is calm, secure, and self-satisfied (low Neuroticism).
Trait characterized by sociability, energy, and talkativeness.
A statistical procedure used to identify clusters of related personality items.
Trait characterized by curiosity, imagination, and independence.
Questionnaires designed to gauge a wide range of feelings and behaviors.
The interacting influences of behavior, internal cognition, and environment.
All our thoughts and feelings about ourselves in answer to Who am I?
One's belief in their ability to succeed in a specific task.
One's overall sense of self-worth or value.
Behavior is influenced by the interaction between traits and social context.
Descriptions of personality based on stable and enduring behavior patterns.
Seeking excitement through travel or non-dangerous novel experiences.
Choosing between two desirable options.
A single option that has both positive and negative qualities.
People are motivated to maintain an optimal level of alertness.
Choosing between two undesirable options.
A low tolerance for routine or repetitive tasks.
Seeking release through social extroversion and lack of restraint.
Physiological needs create tension that motivates an organism to satisfy the need.
The desire to perform a behavior to receive external rewards or avoid punishment.
A hormone secreted by an empty stomach that signals hunger.
The maintenance of a steady internal state.
The brain region that controls hunger, thirst, and body temperature.
Behavior is motivated by a desire for external rewards.
Complex, unlearned behaviors that are rigidly patterned throughout a species.
The desire to perform a behavior for its own internal satisfaction.
A hormone secreted by fat cells that signals satiety (fullness).
Describes internal conflicts between different types of goals.
The perfect amount of stress or excitement needed for peak performance.
The master gland that regulates growth and other endocrine glands.
Motivation is based on the needs for competence, autonomy, and relatedness.
Motivation to seek out novel, complex, and intense experiences.
Seeking excitement through risky physical activities.
The principle that performance increases with arousal only up to a certain point.
The experience or expression of emotion or mood.
The mental interpretation of a situation that determines the emotional response.
The name or interpretation assigned to a physical state of arousal.
Cultural norms that regulate the expression of emotions.
Specific triggers that cause an emotional response.
The idea that facial expressions can influence emotional experiences.
The biological and environmental causes of an emotional state.
The difference between physical arousal and the mental processing of an emotion.
Potentially traumatic events occurring in childhood (0-17 years) that can have long-lasting effects on health and well-being.
The first stage of GAS where the sympathetic nervous system is suddenly activated (heart rate zooms, blood diverted to muscles).
A negative form of stress that occurs when a person feels unable to cope with demands, often leading to fatigue or health issues.
Attempting to alleviate stress by avoiding or ignoring a stressor and attending to emotional needs related to one's stress reaction.
A positive form of stress that results from a challenge and can lead to increased focus, motivation, and performance.
The third stage of GAS where the body’s resources are depleted, making the individual more vulnerable to illness or collapse.
An involuntary physiological reaction to a perceived harmful event, attack, or threat to survival.
Hans Selye's concept of the body's adaptive response to stress in three phases: alarm, resistance, and exhaustion.
A subfield of psychology that provides psychology's contribution to behavioral medicine, focusing on how biological, social, and psychological factors influence health and illness.
High blood pressure; a physical condition often exacerbated by chronic psychological stress.
The weakening of the body's ability to fight off infection, often caused by the release of stress hormones like cortisol.
Attempting to alleviate stress directly by changing the stressor or the way we interact with that stressor.
The second stage of GAS where temperature, blood pressure, and respiration remain high, and the body attempts to cope with the stressor.
The process by which we perceive and respond to certain events, called stressors, that we appraise as threatening or challenging.
Specific events or chronic pressures that place demands on a person or threaten their well-being.
Under stress, people (especially women) often provide support to others (tend) and bond with and seek support from others (befriend).
Emotional strengths that involve the exercise of will to accomplish goals in the face of opposition.
A felt sense of wonder, thankfulness, and appreciation for life and the benefits received from others.
A state of mind or feeling characterized by contentment, love, satisfaction, pleasure, or joy.
Interpersonal strengths that involve tending and befriending others.
Civic strengths that underlie healthy community life.
